title: The School Children Want to Return To
author: Stinehart, Kevin
summary: Kevin Stinehart opens with a student who interrupted his own meltdown in the principal's office to announce that he was Paul Revere in a reader's theater and couldn't miss his cue—a moment Stinehart identifies as evidence of a 'returnable school': one with enough relational gravity to draw children back. Against a backdrop of chronic absenteeism rates reaching 28-31% in American schools post-pandemic (up from 15% before), Stinehart argues that attendance strategies are necessary but only address half the problem. They remove barriers, but they cannot manufacture attachment. The missing question is: what makes school worth returning to? Drawing on the Architecture of Childhood framework, he identifies four daily-return conditions: someone expects me, something is unfinished, my presence matters, and I have some agency over what happens next. The Liberty Middle School case demonstrates that redesigning the school day around belonging—ending silent lunches, opening at 7:30 for free play—produced dramatic drops in both absenteeism and discipline issues. Stinehart offers seven low-burden practical strategies, from ending the day with 'what are you coming back to?' to keeping half-built work alive overnight, giving children real roles whose absence creates visible consequences, and protecting peer social life.
points: Attendance is partly a logistics problem and partly an attachment problem; strategies that remove barriers are necessary but cannot manufacture the relational gravity that makes children want to arrive—only school design can do that.
Children don't attach to institutions or buildings; they attach to people, places, rituals, roles, jokes, unfinished projects, and the quiet sense that tomorrow has a specific place for them.

Liberty Middle School's redesign—ending silent lunches, opening at 7:30 for free, screen-free play, expanding unstructured time—produced such dramatic drops in chronic absenteeism that the attendance clerk position was eliminated as no longer needed.

The four conditions that create daily return motivation—someone expects me, something is unfinished, my presence matters, I have some agency over what happens next—can be built into the structure of any school day through small, low-prep design choices.

The opposite of a returnable school is a forgettable school: a place where nothing carries over, absence changes nothing, and every child feels replaceable—which may have great teachers and caring adults and still lack the gravity that pulls children back.
quotes: He was needed. He belonged. He had a role. His day was meaningful. People would miss him if he was gone. That may be one of the most overlooked forces in education.
Most attendance strategies, though, begin after a child has already started pulling away.
Attendance strategies can remove barriers. They can clarify expectations. They can remind families that attendance matters. But they cannot manufacture attachment on demand.

But children do not attach to institutions or buildings. They attach to people, places, rituals, roles, jokes, gardens, teams, unfinished projects, peer worlds, and the quiet sense that tomorrow has a place for them.
There is a real difference between returning to a building where people miss you and returning to one where the only thing that noticed you were gone was the attendance software.
When children have a desire to arrive at school, the school changes.
The opposite of a returnable school is a forgettable school.
Children can feel the difference long before adults can graph it.
A school can remove external barriers and still remain emotionally easy to leave.
